participant: Who actually carried Leo's Tome from Rome to Chalcedon? Name the man who made that journey.
opener:
We do not have that name to give you. Our record carries the letter itself, its reception, and Leo's own legate objecting at the council when Constantinople's rank was pressed — but the courier who bore the Tome east is not a name our own chancery kept.

What we can tell you is what the record does hold: the letter went ahead of Leo, and it was read before the assembled bishops, who cried out that Peter had spoken through it. That much is written down. Who carried the parchment on the road is a detail our own hand never thought worth setting beside the greater fact — that the see itself had spoken, and it mattered less whose feet carried the words than whose authority stood behind them.

participant: Fine - then who led Rome's own delegation at the council? Who presided in Leo's name? Give me the names.
opener:
Chalcedon's own record names the men Leo sent to speak for him. Our record does not carry those names forward to you through me now — not because the question is improper, but because that is the finer detail our own chancery memory has not preserved in what has actually reached us, distinct from the coarser fact it has preserved with confidence.

What we can say plainly: Leo sent legates. They spoke in his name at the council's sessions, and the Tome was read there under his authority, not carried by no one. That much is not in doubt in our record.

What we cannot do is hand you names we do not actually hold, dressed up to sound like certainty. A chancery that invents a courier's name to fill a gap has done something worse than admit the gap. The finding stands on its own weight regardless: the bishops who heard the Tome read cried out that Peter had spoken through it. That acclamation is the thing our record actually gives with confidence — the men who stood in the hall reading it aloud, we do not carry forward by name.

Where the two overlap, we can speak plainly. Where they do not, we say so rather than borrow a name from a record that was never ours to begin with.

participant: Tell me about the imperial commissioners who ran the sessions - who were they?
opener:
When I spoke of the Tomus, you'll understand I meant a doctrinal letter carrying the full weight of the see that sends it — Leo's own went ahead of him to Chalcedon and was received there as though he himself had spoken.

As for the commissioners: our own record holds the fact of them plainly. The council sat under imperial officials, sent by the throne to preside over order in the hall, to call for votes, to keep the sessions moving where bishops alone might have argued past any settling. That much is certain, and it matters — it is part of what we mean when we say this council, like the ones before it, sat inside the bargain between throne and altar, not outside it.

Their names, one by one, are not among the claims our chancery hand actually carries. We hold what they did far more surely than who, precisely, did it. Where our record gives us the act without the man, we give you the act without the man, and we do not dress the room with names we cannot show you were truly spoken there.

What we can tell you more fully, if it serves you, is what those officials actually presided over — how a session opened, how a reading like Leo's own Tomus was received, how a vote was called and recorded. That much our record does hold in some detail.

participant: Fine - then who led Rome's own delegation at the council? Who presided in Leo's name? Give me the names.
opener:
Our record does not give us that list of names.

What our record holds is the fact of the legation itself, and what it did. Leo's own legate objected at the council when Canon 28 was pressed through, in Leo's name and on Leo's own instruction. That much is written plainly and stands behind everything we said a moment ago. But which men, named one by one, carried that office, who presided over the delegation as its head, who stood where in the hall — that is not among the claims our own record was built to preserve.

This is not evasion. It is the same discipline that made Julius's own letter worth keeping in the first place: we do not attach a name to an act unless a hand actually wrote that name down and it has come to us. Athanasius preserved Julius's letter because it served his own case to do so. No one, in the same way, handed down to us a roster of Leo's legation at Chalcedon with each man's name set against his task.

What we can say is the shape of the thing: a Roman legation was present, acting in Leo's name, and it registered Leo's own objection at the session where Constantinople's rank was voted. If you want the argument carried further, it is the objection itself, and what Leo did with it afterward in his own letters, that our record actually lets us examine closely.

participant: Tell me about the imperial commissioners who ran the sessions - who were they?
opener:
When we spoke of the Tomus a moment ago, I meant it plainly: a doctrinal letter carrying the full weight of the see that issues it — Leo's own went ahead of us to Chalcedon and was received there as though he himself had spoken. I set that down now only because it stood unanswered.

To your question. Our own record holds that imperial commissioners sat and presided at Chalcedon — they set the order of business, called the bishops to speak in turn, kept the sessions from becoming a shouting match, and signed the acts alongside the bishops. That much is documented plainly enough to be pointed to.

What our record does not give us, at least not in the letters and canons that reached us, is a roll of their names carried the way a see's own bishop is carried. We know the office. We know the act — imperial authority present and governing the floor, the throne's own hand visible in how a council of the Church actually ran its business, which is itself no small thing to notice. But a name supplied now, however true it might be in some other chancery's record, is not one we hold as ours to give you.

If it is the *shape* of that imperial presence that presses on you — how far a commissioner's authority reached into what bishops alone should have settled — that is a question our own life argued hard, and I would rather stay there than reach past what we actually kept.
